claims.text: This is a classic yoshoku (Japanese-Western) kitchen built around wheat. Core dishes such as the ebi fry and live horse-mackerel fry are panko-breaded and deep-fried, and the signature hamburger is finished with a flour-thickened demi-glace, so gluten is central to the menu rather than incidental.

No gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or celiac protocol is documented anywhere in available sources. With breaded fried items and roux/demi-glace sauces sharing the same small kitchen, cross-contamination should be assumed. This restaurant is not celiac-safe.

Seasonings are not itemized publicly, but as a Japanese kitchen it is likely to use standard soy sauce (which typically contains wheat) and dashi-based seasonings in various dishes. Anyone strictly avoiding gluten should not assume any savory dish is wheat-free.

There is no vegan or vegetarian offering documented. The menu centers on meat, seafood, eggs, and dairy (hamburger, fries, gratin, omurice), and even vegetable-forward items like the soup and salad are prepared in a kitchen dominated by animal-based stocks, butter, and demi-glace. Vegan cross-contact is effectively unavoidable here.

No allergy-accommodation policy is documented in available sources. Given the counter format and a daily board of 80-plus changing specials, diners with serious allergies should call ahead in Japanese to confirm before booking; the restaurant is reservation-only and books up roughly a month in advance.

The chef sources ingredients personally from trusted producers nationwide and emphasizes quality and food safety, and the open counter lets guests see the kitchen at work, which can make it easier to ask questions about a specific dish in person.

One dish, the mini curry, is noted as being made without added oil or flour, making it gentler on digestion, though this is not a verified gluten-free preparation and the rest of the menu remains wheat-heavy.

This is a wheat-, soy- and dashi-heavy town-Chinese (machi-chuka) menu and is not celiac-safe. Core dishes rely on wheat noodles and flour: ramen/chuka-soba, the signature ankake yakisoba (crisp wheat noodles), fried rice, gyoza wrappers, and battered chicken tempura (tori-ten). No gluten-free accommodation is indicated anywhere.

The kitchen is a small single-operator setup using shared woks and frying oil, so cross-contact between wheat-floured/battered items and everything else should be assumed. Treat as unsuitable for strict gluten avoidance.

The ankake gravies, stir-fries and set meals are seasoned in the standard Japanese-Chinese style, which means soy sauce - and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. The sweet-savory tamago niku itame and the ankake sauces should be treated as containing wheat-based soy sauce.

Not suitable for vegans. Many savory bases lean on a chicken-bone (tori-gara) stock, and even vegetable-forward dishes mix in pork, ham, chikuwa fish cake or egg (e.g., the ankake yakisoba gravy and the egg dishes). Shared woks would also carry meat/seafood cross-contact.

This is a yakitori-and-izakaya counter, not a celiac-safe kitchen. Skewers are grilled over a shared charcoal grill alongside tare-basted (wheat soy sauce) items, and any battered/fried dishes share oil, so cross-contamination with wheat is likely across the menu.

Naturally gluten-free choices may exist if confirmed — sashimi, salt (shio) skewers, and salt-style katsuo tataki without ponzu — but they must be ordered explicitly shio/no-sauce and confirmed with the chef.

Yakitori tare, ponzu for the katsuo tataki, and nabe broths are built on Japanese soy sauce, which typically contains wheat. Assume these sauces contain gluten unless the chef confirms a wheat-free alternative; ordering shio (salt) avoids the tare.

A fish- and meat-forward Tosa izakaya (bonito, chicken, game-fowl hot pot) with bonito dashi throughout — even vegetable dishes likely carry animal-derived stock. There is no documented vegan menu; confirm each item with the chef.
A tiny, owner-run counter where the chef cooks directly in front of you, so you can ask about ingredients and preparation face-to-face — easiest with some Japanese or a translation app.
Wheat is everywhere: this is a whole-wheat bakery with house-milled flour, so flour dust and gluten cross-contact are unavoidable throughout the kitchen. Not safe for celiacs.
Entirely plant-based kitchen with no butter, eggs, or dairy used in any product, so there is no animal cross-contact to worry about.
English is limited and menu labels are mostly Japanese, but staff are reportedly eager to help answer ingredient questions.
100% vegan bakery and café — every bread, baked good, and lunch item is plant-based, so vegans can order anything on the menu with confidence.
Uses soy-based cream and plant milks plus fermented soy yogurt in place of all dairy.

name: 黒豆珈琲のbean's goody（ビーンズグッディ） (Bean's Goody)

claims.text: This is an omnivore kitchen serving ham & cheese, tuna and egg sandwiches alongside its plant-based items, so cross-contact with animal products is possible for vegan diners; confirm preparation when ordering.

The signature black bean coffee is made purely from Tanba black soybeans, is caffeine-free and inherently plant-based and gluten-free, and soy milk is available as a dairy alternative for cafe au lait.
The cafe offers a vegetable burger and has stocked fully vegan baked goods (Seiun Oyatsu) made without animal-derived ingredients.

name: 毘沙門堂 勝林寺 (Bishamondo Shourin-ji (Shourin Temple))

claims.text: No gluten-free handling information is published. Shojin ryori and accompanying wagashi commonly include wheat (soy sauce, fu/wheat gluten, batter, sweets), so cross-contamination cannot be ruled out and must be discussed when reserving.

No statement that wheat-free tamari is used. Shojin cooking typically uses standard wheat-containing soy sauce unless specially arranged, so assume soy sauce contains wheat unless confirmed otherwise.
As a Zen temple kitchen serving only shojin ryori, no meat, fish, eggs or dairy are used on site, which greatly reduces animal cross-contact compared with an omnivore restaurant.

VegeMap notes that visitors should inform staff of dietary requirements and allergies before ordering; the temple takes reservations by phone (075-561-4311) and web form, which is the channel to arrange a vegan and/or allergy-aware meal.
Listed as fully vegan (all-vegan) on Japan VegeMap, consistent with the temple's shojin ryori tradition that excludes all animal products and uses kelp/shiitake dashi rather than fish stock.
Plant-based meals and matcha-with-sweets are prepared in a temple kitchen with no animal-protein cooking, so the risk of meat or fish cross-contact is inherently low.

name: ブランジュリ ロワゾー・ブルー (Boulangerie L'Oiseau Bleu)

claims.text: The bakery sells both gluten-free (rice-flour/sorghum) breads and ancient-wheat breads (spelt, Kamut, einkorn) that contain gluten, baked in the same small owner-run kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat flour is possible; no dedicated gluten-free-only facility is confirmed.
The kitchen is 100% vegan/plant-based — all products are free of eggs, dairy and honey and there are no animal ingredients on site, so there is no animal cross-contact risk.

The shop states all products are free from eggs, dairy and honey and are made to suit people with allergies and dietary restrictions, and the owner is described as very accommodating and willing to discuss ingredients.
Fully vegan (Vege Project / VegeMap certified all-vegan) with a gluten-free core line using organic, pesticide-free rice flour and sorghum; some items are also Low-FODMAP certified.
No animal products anywhere in the kitchen means vegan diners face essentially zero animal cross-contact.

name: ブラウニーブレッドアンドベーグルズ (Browny Bread & Bagels)

claims.text: Dedicated wheat bakery making bagels, bread and focaccia from domestic wheat; gluten is pervasive throughout the kitchen and there are no gluten-free items, so this is unsafe for celiac diners.
At least one variety is a soy-sauce mochi cheese bagel; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

Many bagels and breads are made and baked alongside cheese, cream cheese, honey and dairy varieties on shared equipment, so vegan items are prepared in the same kitchen as animal-product items. Ask staff which specific bagels are egg-free and dairy-free.

A HappyCow vegan-bakery directory entry notes a domestic-wheat bakeshop whose main products are bagels, white bread and focaccia, many of which are vegan-friendly, and that it offers soy milk for drinks.
Everything is baked fresh on site and the small storefront is known for friendly service.
